items.title: Installation
items.text: This page has installation instructions for different pieces of software that you may need while running FACTS experiments.

items.title: FACTS-experiment-builder (FEB)
items.text: FEB is a package from the FACTS project. It is a command line interface (CLI) tool designed to streamline defining FACTS experiments and generating execution scripts to run experiments. Find the installation guide here.

items.title: Docker
items.text: If you choose to run experiments via Docker Compose, Docker must be installed on your machine. Follow Docker's installation instructions here.

items.title: Apptainer
items.text: An alternative to Docker, Apptainer only runs on Linux machines. Follow the Apptainer installation instructions here.

items.title: Python package manager
items.text: This will be necessary to install and run the FACTS-experiment-builder (FEB) package. We recommend using uv but pip or pipx would work as well if you prefer them. See uv installation instructions here.

items.title: git
items.text: Git is used by a command in FEB to clone the FACTS-module-registry to your FACTS workspace. You can find installation instructions here.

items.title: Module Contributor Documentation
items.text: This is the landing page for resources related to contributing a module to the FACTS2 ecosystem.

items.title: Contents
items.text:
• Module Contributor Guide: Start here! An overview of all of the steps required to develop a module for FACTS.
  • FACTS Module Requirements: This page details all of the requirements that a module must satisfy to be added to the FACTS2 framework.
  • Building a FACTS module tutorial: A step-by-step tutorial showing how to build a module that can be run within the FACTS framework.
  • Submitting a module to the FACTS framework tutorial: Instructions for adding a new module to the FACTS framework, includes a section on writing a module yaml and submitting an entry to the module registry.
  • FACTS Output Types: Overview of the objects written at each step of a FACTS experiment.

items.title: Tutorial: Building the gopher-buckets module
items.text:
Note

By the end of this tutorial, we will have created a working module with all of the necessary components listed in the module requirements document. You can find the repository created in this tutorial here.

In this tutorial, we will demonstrate how to build a new FACTS module. We'll take a pretend example, the contribution of gophers dumping buckets of water into the ocean, to sea-level change.

In our made-up example, gophers around the world engage in the activity of dumping buckets of water into the ocean (and this is not captured by any other physical process). We will call it gopher-buckets 🙂.

The process is temperature-dependent and the effect of gophers on sea-level is also modified by the availability of buckets small enough to be carried by a gopher. In our model bucket size is represented by a random variable, \(P\) and temperature by a random variable, \(T\). For the sake of the example, this is a spatially uniform process and our module will generate projections of global mean sea level (GMSL) change due to gophers. ¯\__(ツ)_/¯

Our example module will take input data, including a dataset of temperature projections (generated in the climate step of a FACTS experiment) and a dataset representing $\(P\)$, and several parameters. To be a FACTS module, it must meet the requirements listed in the FACTS module requirements document. We'll now go through creating the module and satisfying each of the requirements.

items.title: 1. Create a repository for the module using the module-template in the fact-sealevel GitHub organization
items.text:
• Click 'Use this template' -> 'Create new repository'
  • Go through repository creation steps, adding a name, description, etc.

We've just created a repository based on the provided template. It comes with several files pre-populated. Most won't need to be edit to match the name of our module but some will.

For a more detailed explanation of the different components and files in the module template, see the module template overview page.

items.title: 2. Clone the repo locally and open in a text editor or IDE
items.text: • We've just created a repository based on the provided template. It comes with several files pre-populated. Most won't need to be edit to match the name of our module but some will.

items.title: 3. Update pyproject.toml
items.text:
In the pyproject.toml file you'll see references to the project name "module-template" on lines 2 and line 16. Replace these with the name of your module, in this case, "gopher-buckets". In addition, add a description and update the author name and email. On line 16, in addition to updating the moduel name, we want to update the package's executable script to be cli.py. Update gopher-buckets = "gopher_buckets:main" to be gopher-buckets = "gopher_buckets.cli:main".

Screenshot of pyproject.toml file with highlights on lines that need to be updated from the initial module template.

items.title: 4. Update module name elsewhere in project
items.text:
There are a few other locations where the original module name is hardcoded:

  1. Rename the folder: src/module_template/ becomes src/module_buckets
  2. In src/module_buckets/__init__.py: Replace "module-template" with "module-buckets" (or just delete this print statement)
  3. In the Dockerfile, replace instances of "module-template" with "gopher-buckets" (Lines 5 and 19).

items.title: 5. Add module dependencies
items.text:
This is where we will add any packages that our module imports to the project virtual environment. The template has a few dependencies such as Click and Xarray pre-loaded. Click is used to built the command-line tool for the module application and Xarray is used in the read/write functions provided in io.py.

For any other package dependency in your module, run `uv add . For example: 

uv add numpy

Then, run uv sync. You'll see that this updates the pyproject.toml and uv.lock files with the dependencies we just added.

items.title: 6. Write / add module scripts
items.text: Now add the model's code to src/gopher_buckets. Note that the module template provides two scripts, io.py and utils.py. io.py contains functions to read and write the projections (module outputs) associated with a FACTS experiment. In the case of the gopher-buckets module, we'll use one of the IO functions (read_climate()) to read the climate data file input object and another, write_gmsl_projections() to write the module output. We can use utils.make_gmsl_projection_ds() to assemble the generated samples into an xarray.Dataset expected by write_gmsl_projections().

items.title: 7. Make the CLI wrapper
items.text:
We now have a module representing our physical model but no entrypoint. For this, we need to build the CLI tool. The module template comes with a pre-added dependency, Click, and a script, cli.py that we will use.

Note

In this example, we demonstrate using the Click CLI tool. If you prefer to use argparse, or another tool, feel free to do that as well.

For every parameter, input and output file in the module, we need to add a Click CLI command option. Once your module scripts are in the src/module_name/, build out cli.py to have options for all necessary parameters. Pass all options to a main() function. Inside the main function, you can call your module functions (See example here).

items.title: 8. Make a Docker Container
items.text:
We will now create a Dockerfile object for our module. First, double-check that there is a Dockerfile in your repository. You will need to update a few lines with the name of your module. Then, ensure Docker is running on your machine. Finally, from the root directory, run docker build -t gopher-buckets .

You should see an output like this:

Caution

The steps above work in many cases but not all. Creating a docker container can get much more complicated so the standard file provided in the template may need tweaking. If you run into trouble, raise an issue or post in the slack!

items.title: 9. Try running your module locally
items.text:
Run locally in the docker container we just created: 

docker run --rm \
    -v ./data/input:/input/:ro \
    -v ./data/output:/output \
    "gopher-buckets" \
    --scenario="ssp126" \
    --climate-data-file="/input/climate.nc" \
    --bucket-size-input-file="/input/bucket_size.csv" \
    --baseyear=2005 \
    --pyear-start=2020 \
    --pyear-end=2150 \
    --pyear-step=10 \
    --nsamps=500 \
    --rng-seed=1234 \
    --coef-a=0.5 \
    --coef-b=0.25 \
    --coef-c=1.01 \
    --coef-m=0.1 \
    --coef-n=0.01 \
    --output-gslr-file="/output/gslr.nc"

If it runs successfully, output data will be written in ./data/output.

items.title: 10. Format
items.text: Make sure justfile is present, run just validate. It may bring up some errors that you need to fix. Check back soon for instructions on how to bypass and/or modify the checks in this file.

items.title: 11. Enable GitHub Actions
items.text:
The module template comes with two GitHub Actions already configured but not enabled. The first, pythonpackage.yaml, runs linting and formatting. The second, container.yaml, is most important. This uploads the module's Docker container image to the fact-sealevel GitHub Packages. Doing so assigns each image a URI that can be referenced to remotely pull a module's container image (so that you do not need to locally download the source code of the FACTS module you want to run).

The files are currently in a directory called ./github/inactive_workflows. Rename this to ./github/workflows. When you push the renamed directory and the config files to your GitHub repository, the GitHub Actions will automatically run.

items.title: 12. Push to GitHub
items.text: Congrats! We've just created a working FACTS 2 module! You'll now want to push your work to GitHub. First, git add all relevant files. Then, run git commit -m 'add a commit msg here' and finally, git push origin branch-name.

items.title: 13. Archive input data
items.text: Input data must be publicly archived with appropriate documentation and references. We recommend creating a Zenodo archive for your module's input data. See Zenodo instructions here.

items.title: 14. Issue a release of your project
items.text:
in progress, check back soon

Versioned releases are important because they create a reference to a snapshot of the mdoule at a point in time. This is critical for referencing the software in publications and ensuring reproducibility. In the near future, this section will have more information about version naming conventions, suggestions on how to organize a changelog and making the actual release. Check back soon!

items.title: Recap
items.text:
In this tutorial, we created a working command line application that generates projections of global mean sea level change due to a made-up physical process, gophers dumping water into the ocean. Our module has its own GitHub repository and a Dockerfile that builds the image associated with the module's software dependencies. We enabled GitHub Actions that builds the image and uploads it to the container registry.

Head to the next tutorial to learn how to make an entry in the FACTS-module-registry for hte module we've just created.

items.title: FACTS Output Types
items.text: Different steps of a FACTS experiment generate different types of projections. The key element of the FACTS framework is that any module can be run in a given step so long as it ingests and returns the expected objects. For example, a module run in the climate step must produce an Xarray xr.Dataset object that looks like ClimateOutput, described below. On this page, you'll find a description of each type and references to provided functions to read and write these objects that you can adopt in your module.

items.title: FACTS Module Contributor Guide
items.text:
Here you'll find an overview of contributing a module to FACTS, including links to detailed instructions for various steps of the process.

Most of the content assumes you already have a module partially developed, or already developed elsewhere and will be porting a version into the FACTS framework.

items.title: Process
items.text: Below are steps and associated documentation and examples to guide you through the process of developing a FACTS module and contributing it to the FACTS framework.

items.title: Step 1: Review FACTS module requirements
items.text: Find the module requirements document here

items.title: Step 2: Create a repository for your module
items.text: We suggest using the module template available on the FACT-Sealevel GitHub organization.

items.title: Step 3: Develop your module
items.text: For a step-by-step guide on building your module, see the module development tutorial.

items.title: Step 4: Add your module to the FACTS module registry
items.text: See the tutorial on submitting a module to the module registry.

items.title: Modules written in other languages
items.text: The examples in this documentation focus on modules that are developed in Python (so far). However, your module does not need to be written in Python to be a part of FACTS. As long as your module generates projections that look like the outputs of other FACTS modules, and, if applicable, ingests projections generated by FACTS modules, it can be a part of the FACTS framework.

items.title: FACTS-wrapper of existing modules
items.text: If you have a module written in another language that you would like to submit to FACTS, it is possible to generate a thin Python wrapper to allow it to run within a FACTS experiment alongside other modules. For an example, see the emulandice2 module. Feel free to reach out to the FACTS development team if you are in this situation, we are happy to work with you to bring your module into FACTS.

items.title: Making changes to your module
items.text:
It is very likely that you will need to make updates to your module after it has been submitted to the FACTS framework. FACTS's modular and flexible design means that no other modules or packages need to be updated to accomodate changes in a particular module, only that module's registry entry.

Important

If you make an update to a module that changes an input file or argument, it is very important that you make the corresponding update in the modules FACTS-module-registry entry!

FACTS/FEB will not start using a new version of a module until the container specified in its module YAML file is updated. Therefore, once changes are made in a module, it is highly recommended that you issue a new release of the module. Then, go through the steps in the FMR tutorial to clone the repo, make updates and open a PR with the changes. Check back soon for more detailed instructions on this step, or don't hesitate to reach out to a member of the FACTS development team.

items.title: Requirements of a FACTS2 module
items.text: This document describes the set of requirements of a module in the FACTS2 ecosystem. Adding a module to the FACTS2 ecosystem means that it can be used by facts-experiment-builder, making it easier for others to configure experiments that include your module. The purpose of this document is to help guide new module contributors through the module development process. Other helpful resources include the example module tutorial and module registry submission tutorial. If you haven't already, review the module templtae provided in the fact-sealevel GitHub organization. The template comes pre-populated with some of the files required for all modules.

items.title: 1. Modules must have an associated GitHub repository
items.text:
• Ideally, the repo is located in the fact-sealevel GitHub org, but if you prefer, it can be located elsewhere.
    • If elsewhere, the repository must be public and it must have permissions for GitHub Packages, which you can read more about here. If you’re unsure about any of this, please reach out to us! We are happy to help figure this part out.

items.title: 2. The module must be a command line application
items.text:
• The modules currently in the FACTS2 ecosystem use Click, which we recommend. However, it is also feasible to use built-in argparse methods if that is your preference (bit about the differences here).
  • If you already have a way of creating and organizing an application that works for you, that is great and you should use what is easiest for you. If you haven’t developed a CLI application or would like some guidance, we will share an example/template that we hope will help guide you through the steps of setting up the module (so you can focus on the science!) (this is in progress)

items.title: 3. Module must have a Docker container image
items.text: • Module contains a Dockerfile with instructions to build a Docker container image of the application. We are happy to help with this step and the FACTS documentation will have instructions for this + an example soon.

items.title: 4. Input data must be archived and publicly available (such as a Zenodo record)
items.text:
• We’re happy to create and submit a Zenodo record for your module input data in the fact-sealevel Zenodo community. If you’d rather archive the data yourself or use something other than Zenodo, that is also fine as long as it has a publicly accessible DOI.
    • Accompanying module input data, there must be instructions to generate that input data. We recommend using this template, but exact guidance is still being developed.

items.title: 5. Module must have an entry in the facts module registry
items.text:
• This means a directory in the registry repo with the module’s name. Directory contains a module yaml (ie. module_name_module.yaml) file.
  • Module yaml must match the schema used by existing modules in the registry.
    • Note: we are working on specific documentation to help with this and will make an empty module yaml that contributors can copy paste as a starting point available soon.

items.title: 6. The module accepts standard forcing inputs and produces standard outputs
items.text: See FACTS Output Types page

items.title: Module Template Overview
items.text: The FACTS project provides a GitHub template repository that can be used to build repositories for new FACTS modules. This template contains a number of files to help get started when creating a new module (for a tutorial on making a new module, ) check out the 'Build a FACTS Module' tutorial. On this page, you'll find an overview of each piece of the module template and what it does.

items.title: src/module_template
items.text: This is the codebase of your module. It holds Python scripts. Important: Must also have a __init__.py file.

items.title: .dockerignore
items.text: Similar to .gitignore, files to be ignored when creating the Docker container image

items.title: .gitignore
items.text: Files to ignore in this repository for git tracking

items.title: .python-version
items.text: Specifices the Python version used in this project.

items.title: CHANGELOG.md
items.text: Used for tracking changes associated with this module. We recommend the Keep a changelog approach for maintaining organized, readable changelogs.

items.title: README.md
items.text: Your module's about page. We recommend following the example laid out in the module template and other modules in the FACTS2 module ecosystem.

items.title: justfile
items.text: This is used to run linting, formatting, tests and other automatic processes.

items.title: pyproject.toml
items.text: The main file defining your project. It is created by running uv init but comes pre-populated when you create a new repository from the module template.

items.title: uv.lock
items.text: A lock file for your project's dependencies.

items.title: Tutorial: Making a gopher-buckets entry in the FACTS-module-registry
items.text:
This tutorial demonstrates how to write an entry in the facts-module-registry for a new module (If you're not familiar with the module registry, we recommend checking out the FACT-sealevel Overview page). We'll continue the example module we used in the previous tutorial and write an entry to add the gopher-buckets module to the FACTS-module-registry.

An entry in the module registry is a directory containing a single YAML file. The YAML file functions as a 'calling card' of the module including the versioned container image holding the module software, and information about input files and arguments, any files written by the module, and how it interacts with other modules in the FACTS2 ecosystem.
path: Tutorial: Making a gopher-buckets entry in the FACTS-module-registry

items.title: Preparation
items.text: Before writing a module YAML, we need the following pieces in place: - A container image of the working module CLI application. (ie. the end point of the previous tutorial) - The output of the module's --help command. Every flag in the CLI command will have its own entry as an argument in the module YAML. - The names of the input files used in the module. These must be set (and must match the filenames used in the publicly archived module input data)

items.title: Arguments section
items.text:
In the arguments section, there is an entry for every flag that is passed to the module CLI. They are divided into sections: "top-level", "options", "fingerprint_params","inputs", and "outputs". You can read more about the different sections in the About Module YAML Files page. What is important to know right now is that each entry must have at least the following fields:

- name: "flag_name" # corresponds to name of CLI flag. "flag_name" becomes --flag-name
  type: #type of arg: str | int | float | bool | file
  source:
source tells FEB where to read for this field from when it creates and pre-populates an experiment config file. If module_inputs, value comes from the module yaml (this file), if metadata, value comes from args passed to the FEB CLI command, setup-experiment.
path: Tutorial: Making a gopher-buckets entry in the FACTS-module-registry

items.title: Volumes section
items.text: The final section of the module YAML lists any named bind mounts that are referenced in the arguments passed to the module. If an entry in the inputs or outputs sub-sections of the arguments section contains mount.volume, it must be listed as a key here. The values, host_path, container_path, and help instruct FEB how to resolve the host and mounted paths and pass the help message describing the volume to the experiment configuration file.

items.title: Open a Pull Request in FACTS-module-registry
items.text: Once you have completed the module YAML file, open a PR in the FACTS-module-registry repo. A maintainer will review it. In the future, we hope to implement a tool to automatically check/validate new module yaml entries.
